summary: The admin check in DeleteUser is inverted. Admins get 403, and any signed-in non-admin can delete any user account. This is an authorization bypass on a destructive, irreversible operation, and it breaks both criteria. The only test covers the unauthenticated 401 path, so neither the admin nor the non-admin path is tested.

findings.title: Inverted admin check: non-admins can delete users and admins are refused
findings.detail: The handler returns 403 when the caller IS an admin and goes on to h.Users.Delete for every other signed-in user. Any authenticated non-admin can delete arbitrary accounts (DELETE /admin/users/{id}), which is irreversible data loss and privilege escalation. Admins cannot use the endpoint. This contradicts the story and criteria 1 and 2.
findings.fix: Change the condition to `if !u.IsAdmin() {` so only admins reach the Delete call.

findings.title: No tests for the admin (204) and non-admin (403) paths
findings.detail: The only test checks 401 for an unauthenticated request. Nothing exercises an admin deleting (204 and Delete called) or a non-admin being refused (403 and Delete not called), which is why the inverted check went unnoticed.
findings.fix: Add table tests with a fake Auth that returns an admin and a non-admin user, and a fake Users store. Assert 204 plus a Delete call for the admin, and 403 with no Delete call for the non-admin.

criteria.evidence: handler.go:28 returns 403 when u.IsAdmin() is true, so an admin gets 403 and user 7 is not deleted.
handler.go:28 lets a non-admin through to h.Users.Delete, which returns 204 and deletes user 7 instead of returning 403.
